newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel unveils German tax reform proposals.
newsitem.headline: Waigel unveils German tax reform proposals.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Friday unveiled his legislative proposals for big corporate and income tax cuts to create new jobs by stimulating the German economy.

The ruling coalition's tax package and pension reforms which are being finalised are the two main economic reforms that Chancellor Helmut Kohl hopes will lay the foundation for a record fifth election victory next year.

Opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who want tax cuts to benefit ordinary workers, opposed the government tax plan, and no date was set for the resumption of talks aimed at resolving differences over tax reform.

Germany, under pressure to cut unemployment from postwar record levels while at the same time containing its budget deficit in order to take part in a single European currency, cannot resort to the age-old method of boosting spending.

Instead, it wants to give companies room to grow by cutting taxes. Tax cut programmes in North America and Britain over the past decade show that they can produce a sounder base of government revenues, Waigel said.

"With these proposals, fiscal policy is showing the way to more growth and jobs in our country," he told a news conference. The reform could boost economic growth by half a percentage point a year and investment by 1.5 points, he said.
By slashing Germany's notoriously high income and corporate tax rates, the proposals would also make the country more attractive to foreign investors, he added.

The tax bills, with up to 30 billion marks ($17.6 billion) in net tax cuts, would eliminate many tax breaks to broaden the tax base and simplify the system. They would also raise indirect taxes such as the value-added tax or petroleum tax to finance part of the income tax cuts.
Waigel said a government spending freeze was still under consideration but that no concrete decision had been made.
The bills contain no substantial changes from a plan announced in January by a coalition panel chaired by Waigel.

While the bulk of the tax reform would take effect in 1999, some parts would start next year and the package could boost the economy this year as companies accelerate investment to take advantage of tax breaks that are set to expire, he said.

Political sparring between Kohl's coalition and the SPD, meanwhile, grew louder. Waigel said he was ready to talk with the SPD at any time about the tax reform but he challenged the opposition to make its own concrete proposals.

Waigel said he hoped the SPD would return to the bargaining table, to avoid having to shepherd the bill through a parliamentary mediation committee later. The SPD has targeted parts of the plan, though it too favours the stimulative impact it aims for.
Kohl also urged the SPD to rejoin the cross-party talks on tax reforms which they broke off a week ago in a clash over coal subsidies.
"The government has made its offer. The SPD has to do the rest," Kohl said before a meeting of his Christian Democrats called to agree a pensions reform policy.
SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine said a majority of Germans opposed the government's plan to slash taxes for top earners.

"A large majority simply does not understand why Chancellor Helmut Kohl calls for wage restraint and the coalition at the same time demands a reform which would bring tax cuts of 20,000 to 30,000 marks a year for the rich," he told parliament.
With its majority in the upper house, the SPD is in a position to block the tax reform bill.

The Federation of Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHT) greeted the bills as a stimulus for more investment and jobs and called on the SPD and the upper house of parliament not to let its beneficial effects get lost in political one-upmanship.
"With this law Germany can impress foreign investors that it is capable of reform and will again become an attractive place to do business," DIHT said.
